items.title: Security report: tari-ootle ootle-wasm / ootle.ts: stealth amounts outside u64 are reduced modulo 2^64 at the WASM boundary, so 2^64 + 5 is built, proven and validated as 5 (ISSUE-2982)
items.evidence: Retro bounty for @okansaglam016161-pixel for reporting a security vulnerability in `tari-ootle` in a GitHub issue: https://github.com/tari-project/tari-ootle/issues/2982. The report showed that ootle-wasm / ootle.ts: stealth amounts outside u64 are reduced modulo 2^64 at the WASM boundary, so 2^64 + 5 is built, proven and validated as 5. The reporter did not touch any shared network. The fix was implemented separately by @sdbondi in tari-project/tari-ootle#2983. **No code work is required here.** Details stay in the advisory until it is publish

items.title: Automations: ask the agent in plain words to schedule something for you
items.evidence: Check whether the agent can set up a schedule from a normal request in a thread. ## Try this 1. In a normal thread, ask: `Every weekday at 8:30 my time, check the top three posts on news.ycombinator.com and give me one line on each. Set that up.` 2. See what the agent does, and whether it asks for your timezone. 3. Open Automations and find what it made. 4. In the same thread, ask it to change the schedule to Mondays only, then to stop it. ## What to look for - The agent sets up the automation, or tells you clearly how to. - What shows on the A

items.title: Automations: run a real recurring job for a week and check it stays useful
items.evidence: Check whether an automation stays useful over several runs. ## Try this 1. Pick something you'd want every day or week: a digest of a topic you follow, new releases of an open-source project you use, or new posts on a blog. 2. Create it in Automations with clear instructions: what to check, what to write, how long, and "say nothing new if nothing changed". 3. Turn it on and let it run at least five times. 4. Read each result. Change the instructions once if something annoys you. ## What to look for - Results stay accurate and on topic, and link

items.title: Automations: edit, pause and delete one, and check what happens to its runs
items.evidence: Check the full life of an automation. ## Try this 1. Create an automation (Automations, New automation) that runs every hour with a small job, and turn it on. 2. After one run, use Edit automation to change the instructions. 3. Pause it, wait past its next run time, then turn it on again. 4. Use Run now while a run is already going. 5. Delete it, then check Active runs and your sidebar. 6. Try the search box and the Active and Paused filters. ## What to look for - The new instructions apply from the next run. - A paused automation doesn't run.

items.title: Automations: set a custom schedule and timezone, and check when it really runs
items.evidence: Check custom cron schedules and timezones on automations. ## Try this 1. In Automations, choose New automation with a custom Cron expression, `*/15 * * * *` (every 15 minutes), and a small job: `Add the current time to a file called ticks.md, one line per run.` 2. Set Timezone to your own, for example Europe/London or Asia/Kolkata. Save and turn it on. 3. Make a second one with `0 9 * * 1-5` and a timezone far from yours. 4. Watch the first runs of each. 5. Try saving an invalid cron and an invalid timezone. 6. Pause or delete the 15 minute one

items.title: Automations: create one, turn it on, and check its first runs
items.evidence: Check setting up a scheduled task on the Automations page. ## Try this 1. Open Automations (app.useagent.org/agent/automations) and choose New automation. 2. What should run: "Daily weather note". Instructions: `Find tomorrow's weather for and write a three-line note on what to wear.` Cadence: Daily. Set your Timezone. 3. Save it. Note its state, then turn it on. 4. Use Run now once. 5. Wait for its first scheduled run, then open View history. ## What to look for - It's clear that new automations start paused, and how to turn one on. - Run now
